title: Justification is instantaneous — present-tense fiducia cannot be required of the pious
source_text: CVII. Sed in eo nimis subtiliter, & minus solide videntur Philosophari. Nam secundum Scholae Reformatae doctrinam, hominis justificatio consistit in indivisibili, & proinde fit in instanti. Quippe in eo sita est, quod simul ac peccator implevit eam conditionem, quam Deus ab eo postulat, ut peccata ipsi remittantur, cessat esse irae divinae obnoxius, & incipit esse Deo gratus, & acceptus ad vitam aeternam, propter Christi meritum & satisfactionem. Sed quomodo potest homo praecise observare & notare illud instans, quo conditio ista primum in eo impleta est, & formata ultima & proxima dispositio ad justificationem, ut in praesenti credat sibi tum remitti peccata? Et si ad justificationem hominis requiritur, ut in praesenti credat sibi peccata remitti, in quos scrupulos necesse est conjici multos viros pios & bonos, qui non potuerunt unquam instans istud animadvertere, in quo ipsis in praesenti peccata remitterentur? Nec quis potest ulla cum ratione negare, in homine seria poenitentia ducto, ad obtinendam a Deo remissionem peccatorum, sufficere syncerum ad Dei misericordiam in Christo perfugium, cum fiducia veniae impetrandae.
pass_a_gloss: But in this they seem to philosophize too subtly and less solidly. For according to the doctrine of the Reformed School, a person’s justification consists in an indivisible, and therefore happens in an instant. Indeed it is situated in this: that as soon as the sinner has fulfilled that condition which God requires of him in order that his sins be remitted, he ceases to be liable to divine wrath and begins to be pleasing to God and accepted to eternal life, on account of Christ’s merit and satisfaction. But how can a person precisely observe and note that instant in which that condition was first fulfilled in him and the last and nearest disposition to justification was formed, so that in the present he believes sins are then being remitted to him? And if for a person’s justification it is required that in the present he believe sins are being remitted to him, into what scruples must many pious and good people be cast who could never notice that instant in which sins were being remitted to them in the present? Nor can anyone with any reason deny that, in a person led by serious repentance, for obtaining remission of sins from God it suffices to have a sincere refuge to God’s mercy in Christ, with trust of obtaining pardon.
pass_b_english: Le Blanc: this triple cut is too subtle. Reformed doctrine holds justification indivisible and instantaneous — the moment the required condition is met, wrath ceases and acceptance begins for Christ’s sake.
No one can clock the instant of that last disposition so as to believe “sins are being remitted to me right now.”
Requiring present-tense fiducia traps many sincere penitents in scruples.
Enough for remission: sincere refuge to God’s mercy in Christ with trust of obtaining pardon.
